---
title: "A local development workflow you can repeat on every project"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [local-dev, workflow, git, ddev]
summary: "Set up a local development workflow that starts clean, stays predictable, and makes context switches easier."
slug: "local-development-workflow"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a local development workflow with [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [DDEV](https://ddev.readthedocs.io/), and [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) so your projects start the same way, stay easy to resume, and break less when you switch tasks.

## Prerequisites

- Git installed and configured
- DDEV installed on your machine
- Visual Studio Code or another editor you already use
- A project with a documented test command

## Start Every Project the Same Way

Your workflow should remove decisions from the first five minutes. If every project starts differently, you waste time remembering details instead of doing the work.

A simple local workflow looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Clone project] --> B[Start local services]
    B --> C[Install dependencies]
    C --> D[Run database setup]
    D --> E[Start coding]
    E --> F[Run tests and linters]
    F --> G[Commit small changes]
```

This diagram gives you a fixed order. That order matters, because the rest of your workflow depends on a clean start.

If your team already has setup notes, turn them into commands you can run without interpretation.

## Use One Command for Project Setup

A good setup command should handle the boring parts in one place. You should not need to remember five separate commands every time you pull a fresh branch.

```bash
ddev start
ddev composer install
ddev exec php artisan migrate
```

This starts your containers, installs PHP dependencies, and applies database changes. If your project uses a different stack, keep the pattern and swap the commands.

If you want fewer manual steps, move that sequence behind a task runner.

```yaml
version: '3'

tasks:
  setup:
    cmds:
      - ddev start
      - ddev composer install
      - ddev exec php artisan migrate
  test:
    cmds:
      - ddev exec php artisan test
```

This gives you one command for setup and one command for verification. That is easier to remember, but it only helps if your daily loop stays just as consistent.

## Keep Your Daily Loop Small

A local workflow gets better when your next action is obvious. You open the project, start services, make a change, run checks, and commit before the work drifts.

```bash
git switch -c fix/login-validation
code .
task test
```

This creates a focused branch, opens the project, and runs your test task. It keeps the work scoped, which matters once you start jumping between issues.

You can make that loop even clearer by separating editing from verification.

## Run Checks Before You Switch Context

Context switches cause sloppy work. The fix is simple: run the same checks every time before you leave a branch, even if you plan to come back later.

```bash
git status --short
task test
git add .
git commit -m "Validate login input"
```

This shows what changed, reruns your checks, and captures a small commit. Small commits are easier to review, and they make interrupted work easier to resume.

If you skip this step, the next session starts with doubt. You need a way to confirm the workflow is still doing what you expect.

## Verify Your Local Development Workflow Works

Your workflow is only useful if you can trust it on an ordinary day. You do not need a perfect system. You need one that starts clean and tells you quickly when something is wrong.

Use this checklist:

- Clone the project into a new directory
- Run your setup command once
- Confirm the app boots locally
- Run the test command
- Make a small change and commit it on a feature branch

{{< callout type="tip" >}}
If one of these steps needs tribal knowledge, your workflow is not finished yet. Put that missing detail into the setup command or project docs.
{{< /callout >}}

A repeatable workflow gives you a cleaner start, faster recovery after interruptions, and fewer "it works on my machine" surprises. Once your setup is stable, the next improvement is usually documentation: write the commands down exactly as you want your future self to use them.

title: "Local-first development keeps your feedback loop honest"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]

summary: "Learn what local-first development changes in your day-to-day work and why it helps when you need faster feedback."

Ahnii!

This post shows you what local-first development gives you, why it matters when your tooling keeps getting in the way, and who benefits most from keeping more of the work on their own machine.

Local-first development is not a retreat from the cloud. It is a way to shorten the path between an idea, a code change, and a result you can trust.

You feel the difference fast. Your app starts without waiting on a flaky network. Your tests fail where you can see them. Your database, queue, and files are close enough to inspect instead of guess at.

That changes how you work.

You stop treating feedback as something that arrives later from CI or a shared staging box. You get it while the code is still warm. That makes small fixes cheaper, but it also changes the kind of systems you are willing to build.

## Why Local-First Development Speeds Up Daily Work

When your development loop depends on remote services for every small check, you spend part of the day waiting for permission to continue. Local-first development removes a lot of that waiting. You run the app, inspect the state, break things on purpose, and recover without asking anyone else for access.

Speed is only the first reason to care, though. The bigger gain is confidence, and that is where the next section needs to go.

---
title: "Migrate your frontend toolchain without breaking your build"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [tooling, migration, vite, webpack]
summary: "Learn how to move from Webpack to Vite in small steps so your build stays predictable."
slug: "migrate-your-frontend-toolchain-without-breaking-your-build"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

If your frontend build feels slow or fragile, this post shows you how to move from [Webpack](https://webpack.js.org/) to [Vite](https://vite.dev/) in small steps without losing your existing entry points, scripts, or deployment flow.

## Prerequisites

- A project that already builds with Webpack
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) installed
- A test or smoke-check command you can run after each change

## Replace Your Build Scripts One Step at a Time

Start by adding the new toolchain beside the old one. That gives you a clean comparison point, but the script names matter.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "build:legacy": "webpack --mode production"
  }
}
```

This keeps your old production build available while you introduce the new one. You can compare outputs before you remove anything.

## Move Entry Points Into Vite Config

Your old bundler usually hid a lot of decisions in one large config file. Split those decisions into the parts you still need.

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import path from 'node:path';

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    rollupOptions: {
      input: {
        app: path.resolve(__dirname, 'resources/js/app.ts'),
        admin: path.resolve(__dirname, 'resources/js/admin.ts')
      }
    }
  }
});
```

This tells Vite which files should remain first-class entry points. If your old build produced separate bundles, this is where you preserve that shape.

## Verify Asset Paths Before You Remove Webpack

A migration usually fails at the edges: file paths, manifest names, and deploy assumptions. Check those before you delete the fallback script.

```bash
npm run build
ls dist
```

Run the new build, then inspect the output directory. You want to confirm that your expected entry files, hashed assets, and static files are all present.

## Verify It Works

Use the same smoke check after every change.

```bash
npm run build
npm test
```

The build confirms your bundling path. The tests catch the parts your bundler config used to mask, which is why this is the point where you decide whether the migration is actually safe.

---
title: "Use a repeatable workflow when a task starts to sprawl"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: ["workflow", "writing"]
tags: ["workflow", "debugging", "process"]
summary: "You will learn a simple workflow for breaking a messy task into steps you can repeat without losing track of what matters."
slug: "repeatable-workflow-plain-language"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to turn a messy task into a repeatable workflow so you can move faster, make fewer guesses, and explain your work clearly.

## Prerequisites

- A task that has more than one moving part
- A place to write short notes, such as a scratch file or notebook
- Enough context to name the goal in one sentence

## Use a Repeatable Workflow Instead of Reacting

When a task feels loose, you do not need more energy. You need a shape.

A repeatable workflow gives you that shape. It keeps you from jumping between ideas, half-fixes, and side quests. But a workflow only helps if you can actually follow it, so keep it short.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Name the goal] --> B[Gather only the needed context]
    B --> C[Pick the next concrete step]
    C --> D[Do the step]
    D --> E[Check the result]
    E --> F{Done?}
    F -- No --> C
    F -- Yes --> G[Summarize what changed]
```

This flow gives you a small loop to stay inside. You are not solving the whole task at once. You are finishing one clear step, then checking what changed.

## Start With a One-Sentence Goal

Write down what you are trying to finish before you touch anything else.

If you cannot say the goal in one sentence, the task is still blurry. Fix that first. The goal does not need to be elegant. It needs to be specific enough that you can tell when you are done.

```text
Goal: turn the draft process into five steps the reader can repeat.
```

This line acts like a boundary. It tells you what belongs in the work and what does not.

## Gather Context Without Drowning in It

Now collect only the information that changes your next step.

That usually means the current draft, the audience, and the constraint that matters most. You are not building a museum of background details. You are getting enough context to act without guessing.

```text
Context
- Audience: readers who want practical writing help
- Problem: the explanation feels flat
- Constraint: keep the language direct and easy to reuse
```

This note is short on purpose. If your context list keeps growing, you are probably delaying the real work, which is choosing the next move.

## Pick the Next Step You Can Actually Finish

Do not ask, "How do I solve all of this?" Ask, "What can I finish in the next pass?"

That shift matters. Big questions create fog. Small questions create motion.

```text
Next step: rewrite one section so each paragraph carries one idea and the cadence changes from line to line.
```

This is the step that moves the draft. The next section shows how to work that step without falling back into autopilot.

## Run the Same Editing Loop Each Time

Use the same loop for every section.

Read the section once. Cut the sentence that only repeats the heading. Shorten the longest line. Add one medium sentence after two short ones if the rhythm feels too even. Then stop and read it out loud.

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Read for the point" >}}
Ask what the paragraph is trying to do. If it has two jobs, split it.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Cut the extra line" >}}
Remove the sentence that restates what the reader already knows. Most flat sections have one.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Change the cadence" >}}
Put a short sentence beside a longer one. Change the opening structure if three sentences in a row sound the same.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Check the result" >}}
Read it back. If the section sounds clearer and moves faster, keep it. If not, run the loop again.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

These steps are simple, but that is the point. You can reuse them tomorrow on a different draft without inventing a new method from scratch.

## Verify the Workflow Is Working

A workflow is useful only if it changes the result.

Check for three things. First, each paragraph should carry one idea. Second, the section should move forward without repeating itself. Third, the sentence rhythm should feel varied enough that the reader does not start predicting every beat.

{{< callout type="tip" >}}
If a section still feels dull after one pass, do not add bigger words. Change the structure first.
{{< /callout >}}

That final check keeps you honest. It also gives you a clean way to revise the next section, because now you know what to look for.

---
title: "Rewrite vague development notes into useful process steps"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development-process]
tags: [documentation, writing, process, engineering]
summary: "Learn how to turn vague process notes into clear steps your team can actually follow."
slug: "rewrite-vague-development-notes"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to turn vague development-process notes into clear instructions so you can keep work moving without hiding behind soft words.

## Prerequisites

- A draft process note, handoff, or retro summary
- A clear reader: your team, your future self, or the next person on call
- Enough project context to name the actual step, decision, or risk

## Spot vague language in process notes

Words like "momentum," "seamless," "robust," and "transformative" sound useful, but they do not tell you what to do next. You need to replace mood words with actions, owners, and checks, but first you need to see how much they hide.

```markdown
We kept momentum by moving to a seamless review flow.

The new handoff process is robust and transformative.

This created better collaboration across the team.
```

This note sounds positive, but it does not name a single behavior. You cannot run it, review it, or repeat it.

## Rewrite each note as a concrete step

A useful process note answers simple questions: who did what, when did it happen, and how do you know it worked. Once you write that down, the next person can follow it instead of guessing.

```markdown
We moved pull request review to a same-day rule.

If a pull request is opened before 2 p.m., one reviewer responds before end of day.

If the reviewer requests changes, the author updates the branch and posts a short summary of what changed.

We treat the pull request as stalled after one business day without review.
```

This version gives you a rule, a deadline, and a failure condition. Now you can measure whether the process exists or whether the note was just trying to sound confident.

## Replace broad claims with observable outcomes

The fastest way to clean up a fuzzy draft is to cut every claim that cannot be checked. If you say a process improved something, show the exact change.

```markdown
Before:
- Reviews happened when someone noticed the pull request.
- Handoffs lived in chat threads.

After:
- Every pull request gets one named reviewer.
- Handoff notes live in the issue before the author signs off.
- Blockers are listed under a "Needs decision" heading.
```

This rewrite keeps the contrast, but it earns it with specific behavior. That also sets up the next move: giving people a format they can reuse.

## Use a process-note template your team can fill in

A template keeps you from drifting back into vague language when work gets busy. It also makes reviews easier because every note answers the same questions.

```markdown
## Change
[What changed?]

## Why
[What problem does this solve?]

## New rule
[What should happen now?]

## Owner
[Who is responsible?]

## Verify
[What tells you this is working?]

## Blockers
[What still needs a decision?]
```

This template forces each note to do real work. If a sentence does not fit one of these fields, it is usually filler.

## Verify your note survives a handoff

The test is simple: can someone else follow the note without asking what you meant. If they cannot, the note still describes a feeling instead of a process.

{{< callout type="tip" >}}
Before you save a process note, highlight every adjective. If the word cannot be checked in a pull request, issue, runbook, or calendar rule, cut it or replace it.
{{< /callout >}}

That is the standard to keep. Your note should tell the next person what to do, what to look for, and what still needs a decision.

```bash
find skills -name SKILL.md
```

```markdown
---
name: release-notes

# Release Notes

Write release notes that tell you what changed, why it matters, and what action to take.
```

Start with one file that describes the defaults for every environment. Keep it small. Put shared values here and leave secrets out.

```yaml
app:
  name: inventory-service
  log_level: info
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
database:
  host: localhost
  port: 5432
  name: inventory
feature_flags:
  audit_log: true
```

This file gives your application a stable starting point. You can load it first, then layer environment-specific values on top.

## Override Settings Per Environment

Add a second file for values that change between local development, staging, and production. That keeps your base config readable and makes overrides obvious.

```yaml
app:
  log_level: debug
database:
  host: dev-db.internal
feature_flags:
  audit_log: false
```

This override changes only the keys you need. Everything else still comes from the base file.

## Load Environment Variables Last

Use environment variables for secrets and one-off deployment values. They should win over file-based settings.

```bash
export APP_LOG_LEVEL=warn
export DATABASE_PASSWORD='replace-me'
export SERVER_PORT=9090
```

These variables let you change behavior without editing tracked files. That matters in CI, containers, and production hosts where you want the same config files but different runtime values.

## Merge Configuration in a Clear Order

Load configuration in one direction and keep that order consistent: base file, environment file, then environment variables. If you change the order, you make debugging harder.

```php
<?php

$config = loadConfig('config/base.yaml');
$config = mergeConfig($config, loadConfig('config/development.yaml'));
$config = mergeEnv($config, 'APP_', [
    'APP_LOG_LEVEL' => 'app.log_level',
    'DATABASE_PASSWORD' => 'database.password',
    'SERVER_PORT' => 'server.port',
]);
```

This flow keeps defaults predictable and overrides explicit. When a value looks wrong, you know exactly where to check first.

## Validate Required Keys Before Boot

Fail early if a required setting is missing. Do not wait until the first database call or external request.

```php
<?php

assertConfig($config, [
    'app.name',
    'server.port',
    'database.host',
    'database.password',
]);
```

This validation step turns a vague runtime failure into a direct startup error. You get a shorter feedback loop and a cleaner deploy process.

## Inspect the Effective Configuration Safely

Print the final merged configuration when you need to debug. Mask secrets before you log or display anything.

```bash
php bin/app config:debug
```

Use this command to confirm which values actually loaded. If the output is masked and ordered, you can spot bad overrides fast without exposing credentials.

# Package Overview

This package gives you the core pieces you need to define, store, and query your application data.

## Start With Structured Data

You use this package when your project needs data with clear rules. You define types, set field constraints, and keep storage behavior predictable.

That gives you one place to shape your data model instead of scattering validation and persistence logic across the codebase.

## Define Behavior in Code

You describe your data structures in code. You decide which fields exist, which values are required, and how records relate to each other.

That keeps the rules visible. It also makes changes easier to review, test, and ship.

## Store and Retrieve Records Consistently

You create records through the same model definitions you use to read them. The package handles the common storage flow so you can focus on the rules that matter to your application.

You spend less time wiring basic CRUD behavior by hand. You spend more time shaping the parts that are specific to your project.

## Keep Validation Close to the Model

You attach validation rules where the data is defined. Required fields, allowed values, and relationship checks stay next to the model instead of drifting into controllers or form handlers.

That makes errors easier to trace. It also reduces duplicate checks in different parts of the app.

## Build on a Clear Package Boundary

You can treat this package as the data layer for one concern in your system. It gives you a clean boundary for models, validation rules, and storage behavior.

That matters when the project grows. You can change the internals of the package without rewriting every caller.

## Use It When You Need Predictable Data Rules

Choose this package when you need structured records, repeatable validation, and code-level control over how data behaves.

If your project already has ad hoc arrays, duplicated checks, or storage logic spread across multiple files, this package gives you a cleaner starting point.
